claim: MR1 presents riboflavin- and folate-related metabolites to mucosal-associated invariant T cells.
source: MHC class I-related molecule MR1 presents riboflavin- and folate-related metabolites to mucosal-associated invariant T cells, but it is unknown whether MR1 can present alternative antigens to other T cell lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work in the introduction.

claim: MR1-restricted T cells (MR1T cells) displaying diverse TCRs and reacting to MR1-expressing cells in the absence of microbial ligands were identified in healthy individuals.
source: In healthy individuals we identified MR1-restricted T cells (named MR1T cells) displaying diverse TCRs and reacting to MR1-expressing cells in the absence of microbial ligands.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: MR1T cell clones showed specificity for distinct cell-derived antigens.
source: Analysis of MR1T cell clones revealed specificity for distinct cell-derived antigens and alternative transcriptional strategies for metabolic programming, cell cycle control and functional polarization following antigen stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing different MR1T cell clones recognizing different fractions from cell lysates.

claim: MR1T cell clones exhibited alternative transcriptional strategies for metabolic programming, cell cycle control and functional polarization following antigen stimulation.
source: Analysis of MR1T cell clones revealed specificity for distinct cell-derived antigens and alternative transcriptional strategies for metabolic programming, cell cycle control and functional polarization following antigen stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data and transcription factor network analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: MR1T cell clones showed multiple chemokine receptor expression profiles.
source: Phenotypic and functional characterization of MR1T cell clones showed multiple chemokine receptor expression profiles and secretion of diverse effector molecules, suggesting functional heterogeneity.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing differential expression of CXCR3, CCR4, and CCR6.

claim: MR1T cell clones secreted diverse effector molecules.
source: Phenotypic and functional characterization of MR1T cell clones showed multiple chemokine receptor expression profiles and secretion of diverse effector molecules, suggesting functional heterogeneity.
evidence: This is supported by multiplex cytokine assay data showing variable expression of Th1, Th2, and Th17 cytokines.

claim: MR1T cells exhibited distinct T helper-like capacities upon MR1-dependent recognition of target cells expressing physiological levels of surface MR1.
source: Accordingly, MR1T cells exhibited distinct T helper-like capacities upon MR1-dependent recognition of target cells expressing physiological levels of surface MR1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing MR1T cells inducing DC maturation and modulating intestinal epithelial cell functions.

claim: MR1T cells are a normal part of the human T cell repertoire.
source: These data extend the role of MR1 beyond microbial antigen presentation and indicate MR1T cells are a normal part of the human T cell repertoire.
evidence: This is inferred from the detection of MR1T cells in multiple healthy donors and their estimated frequency in blood.

claim: T lymphocytes can detect lipids presented by non-polymorphic CD1 molecules.
source: T lymphocytes can detect a diverse range of microbial and self-antigens, including lipids presented by non-polymorphic CD1 molecules (Zajonc and Kronenberg, 2007), and phosphorylated isoprenoids bound to Butyrophilin 3A1 (Sandstrom et al., 2014; Vavassori et al., 2013), which stimulate TCR Vγ9-Vδ2 cells, the major population of TCR γδ cells in human blood.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylated isoprenoids bound to Butyrophilin 3A1 stimulate TCR Vγ9-Vδ2 cells.
source: T lymphocytes can detect a diverse range of microbial and self-antigens, including lipids presented by non-polymorphic CD1 molecules (Zajonc and Kronenberg, 2007), and phosphorylated isoprenoids bound to Butyrophilin 3A1 (Sandstrom et al., 2014; Vavassori et al., 2013), which stimulate TCR Vγ9-Vδ2 cells, the major population of TCR γδ cells in human blood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TCR Vγ9-Vδ2 cells are the major population of TCR γδ cells in human blood.
source: T lymphocytes can detect a diverse range of microbial and self-antigens, including lipids presented by non-polymorphic CD1 molecules (Zajonc and Kronenberg, 2007), and phosphorylated isoprenoids bound to Butyrophilin 3A1 (Sandstrom et al., 2014; Vavassori et al., 2013), which stimulate TCR Vγ9-Vδ2 cells, the major population of TCR γδ cells in human blood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MAIT cells are restricted to MHC I-related protein MR1.
source: The repertoire of T cells specific for non-peptide antigens was expanded to include mucosal associated invariant T (MAIT) cells, which are restricted to MHC I-related protein MR1 and were originally described within mouse gut (Treiner et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MAIT cells were originally described within mouse gut.
source: The repertoire of T cells specific for non-peptide antigens was expanded to include mucosal associated invariant T (MAIT) cells, which are restricted to MHC I-related protein MR1 and were originally described within mouse gut (Treiner et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MAIT cells react to different bacteria by recognizing non-proteinaceous antigens.
source: Elegant functional studies showed that MAIT cells react to different bacteria by recognizing non-proteinaceous antigens (Gold et al., 2010; Le Bourhis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The stimulatory antigens for MAIT cells were identified as small riboflavin precursors produced by a wide range of yeasts and bacteria.
source: Finally, the stimulatory antigens were identified as small riboflavin precursors produced by a wide range of yeasts and bacteria (Corbett et al., 2014; Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012; Soudais et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MAIT cells display one of three alternative semi-invariant TCRs in which the TRAV1-2 gene is rearranged with genes encoding TRAJ33, J12 or J20.
source: MAIT cells display one of three alternative semi-invariant TCRs in which the TRAV1-2 gene is rearranged with genes encoding TRAJ33, J12 or J20 (Gold et al., 2014; Lepore et al., 2014; Reantragoon et al., 2012), and is combined with an oligoclonal TCR-β repertoire (Lepore et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MAIT cell TCRs are combined with an oligoclonal TCR-β repertoire.
source: MAIT cells display one of three alternative semi-invariant TCRs in which the TRAV1-2 gene is rearranged with genes encoding TRAJ33, J12 or J20 (Gold et al., 2014; Lepore et al., 2014; Reantragoon et al., 2012), and is combined with an oligoclonal TCR-β repertoire (Lepore et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cells expressing MAIT cell TCRs are frequent in human blood, kidney and intestine.
source: Cells expressing these evolutionary-conserved TCRs are frequent in human blood, kidney and intestine, and comprise a major fraction of T cells resident in the liver (Dusseaux et al., 2011; Lepore et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MAIT cells comprise a major fraction of T cells resident in the liver.
source: Cells expressing these evolutionary-conserved TCRs are frequent in human blood, kidney and intestine, and comprise a major fraction of T cells resident in the liver (Dusseaux et al., 2011; Lepore et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Following activation, MAIT cells release an array of pro-inflammatory and immunomodulatory cytokines.
source: Following activation, MAIT cells release an array of pro-inflammatory and immunomodulatory cytokines, and can mediate direct killing of microbe-infected cells (Dusseaux et al., 2011; Kurioka et al., 2015; Le Bourhis et al., 2013; Lepore et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MAIT cells can mediate direct killing of microbe-infected cells.
source: Following activation, MAIT cells release an array of pro-inflammatory and immunomodulatory cytokines, and can mediate direct killing of microbe-infected cells (Dusseaux et al., 2011; Kurioka et al., 2015; Le Bourhis et al., 2013; Lepore et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MR1 is a non-polymorphic MHC I-like protein.
source: MR1 is a non-polymorphic MHC I-like protein that is expressed at low to undetectable levels on the surface of many cell types (Huang et al., 2008; Miley et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MR1 is expressed at low to undetectable levels on the surface of many cell types.
source: MR1 is a non-polymorphic MHC I-like protein that is expressed at low to undetectable levels on the surface of many cell types (Huang et al., 2008; Miley et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Following bacterial infection, antigen-presenting cells up-regulate surface expression of MR1 due to protein stabilization upon antigen binding.
source: Following bacterial infection, antigen-presenting cells (APC) up-regulate surface expression of MR1 due to protein stabilization upon antigen binding (Huang et al., 2008; McWilliam et al., 2016; Miley et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MR1 is highly conserved across multiple species.
source: MR1 is highly conserved across multiple species, with human and mouse MR1 sharing >90% sequence homology at the protein level (Riegert et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Human and mouse MR1 share >90% sequence homology at the protein level.
source: MR1 is highly conserved across multiple species, with human and mouse MR1 sharing >90% sequence homology at the protein level (Riegert et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MR1-bound ligands reported to stimulate MAIT cells include three ribityl lumazines (RLs).
source: To date, the MR1-bound ligands reported to simulate MAIT cells include three ribityl lumazines (RLs), microbial pterin-like compounds displaying a ribitol at carbon 8 (Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012), and two unstable adducts formed by non-enzymatic reaction of microbial 5-ribityl amino uracil (5-RAU) with either host-derived or bacterial carbonyls such as glyoxal or methyl-glyoxal (Corbett et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MR1-bound ligands reported to stimulate MAIT cells include two unstable adducts formed by non-enzymatic reaction of microbial 5-ribityl amino uracil (5-RAU) with either host-derived or bacterial carbonyls such as glyoxal or methyl-glyoxal.
source: To date, the MR1-bound ligands reported to simulate MAIT cells include three ribityl lumazines (RLs), microbial pterin-like compounds displaying a ribitol at carbon 8 (Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012), and two unstable adducts formed by non-enzymatic reaction of microbial 5-ribityl amino uracil (5-RAU) with either host-derived or bacterial carbonyls such as glyoxal or methyl-glyoxal (Corbett et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: RLs bind to MR1 via hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions with amino acids in the antigen binding cleft.
source: RLs bind to MR1 via hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions with amino acids in the antigen binding cleft (Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012; Patel et al., 2013), whereas binding of unstable 5-RAU-derivatives requires covalent trapping within the MR1 pocket via formation of a Schiff base with Lysine 43 (Corbett et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Binding of unstable 5-RAU-derivatives to MR1 requires covalent trapping within the MR1 pocket via formation of a Schiff base with Lysine 43.
source: RLs bind to MR1 via hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions with amino acids in the antigen binding cleft (Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012; Patel et al., 2013), whereas binding of unstable 5-RAU-derivatives requires covalent trapping within the MR1 pocket via formation of a Schiff base with Lysine 43 (Corbett et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: 6-formyl-pterin (6-FP), acetyl-6-formyl-pterin (Ac-6-FP), and acetylamino-4-hydoxy-6-formylpteridine dimethyl acetal bind MR1 via the same mechanism as 5-RAU derivatives.
source: While three additional molecules have also been demonstrated to bind MR1 via the same mechanism, including 6-formyl-pterin (6-FP), acetyl-6-formyl-pterin (Ac-6-FP), and acetylamino-4-hydoxy-6-formylpteridine dimethyl acetal (Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012; Patel et al., 2013; Soudais et al., 2015), these compounds lack the ribityl moiety necessary for MAIT cell activation and instead inhibit stimulation by microbial ligands (Corbett et al., 2014; Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012; Soudais et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: 6-FP, Ac-6-FP, and acetylamino-4-hydoxy-6-formylpteridine dimethyl acetal lack the ribityl moiety necessary for MAIT cell activation and instead inhibit stimulation by microbial ligands.
source: While three additional molecules have also been demonstrated to bind MR1 via the same mechanism, including 6-formyl-pterin (6-FP), acetyl-6-formyl-pterin (Ac-6-FP), and acetylamino-4-hydoxy-6-formylpteridine dimethyl acetal (Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012; Patel et al., 2013; Soudais et al., 2015), these compounds lack the ribityl moiety necessary for MAIT cell activation and instead inhibit stimulation by microbial ligands (Corbett et al., 2014; Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012; Soudais et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: 6-FP and Ac-6-FP can stimulate a second population of 'atypical' MR1-restricted T cells in the blood of healthy human donors.
source: A recent study reported that 6-FP and Ac-6-FP can also stimulate a second population of 'atypical' MR1-restricted T cells of unknown function in the blood of healthy human donors (Gherardin et al., 2016), but this population, did not express the canonical TRAV1-2 gene which defines MAIT cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The 'atypical' MR1-restricted T cells stimulated by 6-FP and Ac-6-FP did not express the canonical TRAV1-2 gene which defines MAIT cells.
source: A recent study reported that 6-FP and Ac-6-FP can also stimulate a second population of 'atypical' MR1-restricted T cells of unknown function in the blood of healthy human donors (Gherardin et al., 2016), but this population, did not express the canonical TRAV1-2 gene which defines MAIT cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: T cell clone DGB129 recognized cell lines constitutively displaying surface MR1 in the absence of any exogenously added antigens.
source: This T cell clone (DGB129) recognized cell lines constitutively displaying surface MR1 (CCRF-SB lymphoblastic leukemia cells, or THP-1 monocytic leukemia cells; Figure 1A) or A375 melanoma cells (A375-MR1) transfected with an MR1-β2m fusion gene construct (Lepore et al., 2014) (Figure 1A) in the absence of any exogenously added antigens (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Sterile recognition of MR1+ target cells by DGB129 was fully inhibited by blocking with anti-MR1 monoclonal antibodies.
source: Sterile recognition of MR1+ target cells was fully inhibited by blocking with anti-MR1 monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) (Figure 1B), and thus resembled the MAIT cell response to E. coli-derived antigens assessed in parallel (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DGB129 T cells failed to recognize the synthetic MAIT cell agonist 6,7-dimethyl-8-D-ribityllumazine (RL-6,7-diMe).
source: Importantly, DGB129 T cells also failed to recognize the synthetic MAIT cell agonist 6,7-dimethyl-8-D-ribityllumazine (RL-6,7-diMe; Figure 1D) (Kjer-Nielsen et al., 2012), differently from a control MAIT cell clone, which instead was stimulated in MR1-dependent manner by this compound (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: DGB129 cells displayed a TCRαβ heterodimer comprising TRAV29/DV5 rearranged to TRAJ23 and TRBV12-4 rearranged to TRBJ1-1.
source: Unlike the canonical semi-invariant TCR typical of MAIT cells, DGB129 cells displayed a TCRαβ heterodimer comprising TRAV29/DV5 rearranged to TRAJ23 and TRBV12-4 rearranged to TRBJ1-1.
evidence: This is supported by TCR gene sequencing data.

claim: Expression of DGB129 TCRα and β genes in a TCR-deficient cell line conferred MR1 reactivity in the absence of exogenous antigens.
source: Expression of these TCRα and β genes in a TCR-deficient cell line (SKW-3 T lymphoblastic leukemia) conferred MR1 reactivity in the absence of exogenous antigens comparable to that displayed by DGB129 cells (Figure 1F), while in control experiments, transduction of TCRα and β genes of a representative MAIT cell clone conferred the ability to recognize the same target cells in MR1-dependent manner only in the presence of E. coli antigens (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A major fraction of T cell clones from two donors displayed specific recognition of A375-MR1 cells.
source: In both donors we found that a major fraction of T cell clones (126/195 and 37/57, respectively) displayed specific recognition of A375-MR1 cells (Figure 2B,D), which was potently inhibited by anti-MR1 blocking mAbs (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: Recognition of A375-MR1 cells by T cell clones was potently inhibited by anti-MR1 blocking mAbs.
source: In both donors we found that a major fraction of T cell clones (126/195 and 37/57, respectively) displayed specific recognition of A375-MR1 cells (Figure 2B,D), which was potently inhibited by anti-MR1 blocking mAbs (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and 2E.

claim: Twelve MR1-reactive T cell clones expressed seven different TRBV chains.
source: Staining with TCR Vβ-specific mAbs of 12 MR1-reactive T cell clones revealed that they expressed seven different TRBV chains (TRBV4-3, 6-5/6-6/6-9, 9, 18, 25–1, 28, 29–1) with some of the clones sharing the same TRBV gene.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and TCR gene analysis data.

claim: None of the twelve MR1-reactive T cell clones expressed the TRAV1-2 chain, canonical for MAIT cells.
source: Furthermore, none expressed the TRAV1-2 chain, canonical for MAIT cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and TCR gene analysis data.

claim: The percentage of CD69highCD137+ T cells detected was consistently higher after stimulation with A375-MR1 cells than after co-culture with A375-WT cells in all five donors screened.
source: In all of the five donors screened, the percentage of CD69highCD137+ T cells detected was consistently higher after stimulation with A375-MR1 cells (range 0.034–0.072% of T cells) than after co-culture with A375-WT cells (range 0.015–0.032%) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The circulating T cell pool of the analyzed individuals contained A375-MR1-reactive T cells at frequency ranging between 1:2500 and 1:5000.
source: Using this approach, we estimated that the circulating T cell pool of the analyzed individuals contained A375-MR1-reactive T cells at frequency ranging between 1:2500 (0.072–0.032 = 0.04%) and 1:5000 (0.034–0.015 = 0.019%).
evidence: This is calculated from flow cytometry data and represents an estimate.

claim: 31 out of 96 screened T cell clones from Donor C displayed specific reactivity to A375-MR1 cells.
source: Indeed, 31 out of 96 screened T cell clones (32%) displayed specific reactivity to A375-MR1 cells (Figure 3C), which was inhibited by anti-MR1 mAbs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Reactivity of T cell clones to A375-MR1 cells was inhibited by anti-MR1 mAbs.
source: Indeed, 31 out of 96 screened T cell clones (32%) displayed specific reactivity to A375-MR1 cells (Figure 3C), which was inhibited by anti-MR1 mAbs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Representative T cell clones derived from three donors displayed diverse TCRα and β chains.
source: Detailed analysis of representative T cell clones derived from three donors confirmed that they displayed diverse TCRα and β chains and indicated differential expression of CD4, CD8 and CD161 (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Representative T cell clones derived from three donors indicated differential expression of CD4, CD8 and CD161.
source: Detailed analysis of representative T cell clones derived from three donors confirmed that they displayed diverse TCRα and β chains and indicated differential expression of CD4, CD8 and CD161 (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: A control MAIT cell clone reacted to A375-MR1 cells only in the presence of E. coli lysate.
source: While a control MAIT cell clone reacted to A375-MR1 cells only in the presence of E. coli lysate, activation of different MR1T cell clones was not enhanced by the E. coli lysate (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Activation of different MR1T cell clones was not enhanced by E. coli lysate.
source: While a control MAIT cell clone reacted to A375-MR1 cells only in the presence of E. coli lysate, activation of different MR1T cell clones was not enhanced by the E. coli lysate (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MR1-negative A375-WT cells failed to stimulate either MR1T or MAIT cells, irrespective of whether E. coli lysate was added.
source: Consistent with these data, MR1-negative A375-WT cells failed to stimulate either type of T cell, irrespective of whether E. coli lysate was added (Figure 4A) and importantly, anti-MR1 mAbs efficiently blocked both MR1T and MAIT cell responses (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Anti-MR1 mAbs efficiently blocked both MR1T and MAIT cell responses.
source: Consistent with these data, MR1-negative A375-WT cells failed to stimulate either type of T cell, irrespective of whether E. coli lysate was added (Figure 4A) and importantly, anti-MR1 mAbs efficiently blocked both MR1T and MAIT cell responses (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MR1T cell stimulation was impaired in the presence of 6-FP or Ac-6-FP ligands.
source: MR1T cell stimulation was impaired in the presence of 6-FP or Ac-6-FP ligands, which also impaired E. coli stimulation of control MAIT cells, but did not disrupt TCR γδ cell responses to cognate antigen presented by the same APCs (Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 6-FP or Ac-6-FP failed to inhibit the activation of MR1T cells or MAIT cells when the target A375 cells were transduced to express mutant MR1 molecules with defective ligand binding capacity.
source: Notably, 6-FP or Ac-6-FP failed to inhibit the activation of MR1T cells or MAIT cells when the target A375 cells were transduced to express mutant MR1 molecules with defective ligand binding capacity (blockade of Schiff base formation with ligands by mutation of Lysine 43 into Alanine, A375-MR1 K34A; Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: MR1T cells do not recognize 6-FP and Ac-6-FP.
source: The specific inhibition observed with 6-FP or Ac-6-FP indicated that MR1T cells (i) do not recognize 6-FP and Ac-6-FP; (ii) react to MR1-bound cellular antigens; (iii) are stimulated by ligands that do not require the formation of a Schiff base with MR1.
evidence: This is inferred from the inhibition experiments with 6-FP and Ac-6-FP.

claim: MR1T cells react to MR1-bound cellular antigens.
source: The specific inhibition observed with 6-FP or Ac-6-FP indicated that MR1T cells (i) do not recognize 6-FP and Ac-6-FP; (ii) react to MR1-bound cellular antigens; (iii) are stimulated by ligands that do not require the formation of a Schiff base with MR1.
evidence: This is inferred from the inhibition experiments with 6-FP and Ac-6-FP.

claim: MR1T cells are stimulated by ligands that do not require the formation of a Schiff base with MR1.
source: The specific inhibition observed with 6-FP or Ac-6-FP indicated that MR1T cells (i) do not recognize 6-FP and Ac-6-FP; (ii) react to MR1-bound cellular antigens; (iii) are stimulated by ligands that do not require the formation of a Schiff base with MR1.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments with K43A mutant MR1 molecules.

claim: Both THP-1 and A375-MR1 cells grown in RPMI 1640 or in PBS showed the same stimulatory capacity for DGB129 MR1T cells.
source: Both THP-1 and A375-MR1 cells grown in RPMI 1640 or in PBS showed the same stimulatory capacity (Figure 5A,B), thus indicating that medium constituents are not responsible for MR1T cell activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Medium constituents are not responsible for MR1T cell activation.
source: Both THP-1 and A375-MR1 cells grown in RPMI 1640 or in PBS showed the same stimulatory capacity (Figure 5A,B), thus indicating that medium constituents are not responsible for MR1T cell activation.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments comparing cells grown in RPMI 1640 versus PBS.

claim: The DGB129 clone reacted only to fraction N4, containing highly hydrophilic compounds isolated from both freshly explanted mouse tumor and in vitro cultured THP-1 cells.
source: The DGB129 clone reacted only to fraction N4, containing highly hydrophilic compounds isolated from both freshly explanted mouse tumor and in vitro cultured THP-1 cells (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: DGB70 cells recognized fraction N3 and not N4.
source: We also tested the fractions generated from THP-1 lysates with DGB70, another representative MR1T cell clone. DGB70 cells recognized fraction N3 and not N4, (Figure 5E), suggesting that at least two distinct compounds differentially stimulated the two MR1T clones.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: At least two distinct compounds differentially stimulated the two MR1T clones DGB129 and DGB70.
source: We also tested the fractions generated from THP-1 lysates with DGB70, another representative MR1T cell clone. DGB70 cells recognized fraction N3 and not N4, (Figure 5E), suggesting that at least two distinct compounds differentially stimulated the two MR1T clones.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential recognition of fractions N3 and N4 by DGB129 and DGB70 clones.

claim: Fractions N3 and N4 loaded onto plastic-bound MR1 molecules showed alternative and specific stimulatory capacity.
source: The same fractions were also loaded onto plastic-bound MR1 molecules and showed alternative and specific stimulatory capacity, i.e. N3 stimulated only DGB70 cells, while N4 stimulated only DGB129 cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In the absence of N3 and N4 fractions, the two clones DGB129 and DGB70 did not react to MR1.
source: In the absence of N3 and N4 fractions, the two clones did not react to MR1, further indicating the requirement of specific antigens.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: MR1T cells with different antigen specificities are present in the same individual.
source: As DGB129 and DGB70 clones were isolated from the same donor, these findings also suggested that MR1T cells with different antigen specificities are present in the same individual.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that DGB129 and DGB70 clones recognize different antigens and were isolated from the same donor.

claim: DGB129 cells upregulated 403 genes and downregulated 413 genes upon stimulation with MR1+ APCs.
source: The RNA-seq datasets revealed that MR1+ APC stimulated DGB129 cells upregulated 403 genes and downregulated 413 genes, whereas DGB70 cells up-regulated 432 genes and down-regulated 285 genes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data.

claim: DGB70 cells up-regulated 432 genes and down-regulated 285 genes upon stimulation with MR1+ APCs.
source: The RNA-seq datasets revealed that MR1+ APC stimulated DGB129 cells upregulated 403 genes and downregulated 413 genes, whereas DGB70 cells up-regulated 432 genes and down-regulated 285 genes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data.

claim: Some master transcription factors were shared between MR1T cell clones DGB129 and DGB70, whereas others appeared to be clone-specific.
source: This approach showed that some master transcription factors were shared between MR1T cell clones, whereas others appeared to be clone-specific (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by transcription factor network analysis shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Both DGB129 and DGB70 T cell clone responses were identified as being regulated by genes TBX21, FOXP3, FOS, RXRA, FOSL2, IRF4, BATF and TRIB1.
source: Whether assessed for betweenness centrality or tested by the PageRank algorithm, both T cell clone responses were identified as being regulated by genes TBX21, FOXP3, FOS, RXRA, FOSL2, IRF4, BATF and TRIB1.
evidence: This is supported by transcription factor network analysis.

claim: DGB129 cells were further influenced by expression of MYC, HSP90AB1 and CREM.
source: However, while DGB129 cells were further influenced by expression of MYC, HSP90AB1 and CREM, DGB70 cells were instead regulated by EGR1, JUNB, and SREBF1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by transcription factor network analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: DGB70 cells were regulated by EGR1, JUNB, and SREBF1.
source: However, while DGB129 cells were further influenced by expression of MYC, HSP90AB1 and CREM, DGB70 cells were instead regulated by EGR1, JUNB, and SREBF1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by transcription factor network analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: All MR1T cell clones tested released IFN-γ upon stimulation by A375-MR1 APCs.
source: All clones tested released IFN-γ (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), probably as a consequence of in vitro expansion (Becattini et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MR1T cell clones displayed diverse expression profiles of Th1, Th2 and Th17 cytokines, and other soluble factors.
source: However, we also observed diverse expression profiles of Th1 (IL-2, TNF-α and TNF-β), Th2 (IL-3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-10, IL-13) and Th17 cytokines (IL-17A, G-CSF, GM-CSF), and other soluble factors (MIP-1β, soluble CD40L, PDGF-AA and VEGF; Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by multiplex cytokine assay data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Clone DGA4 secreted large quantities of IL-17A, IL-6, TNF-α and GM-CSF, but failed to secrete the prototypic Th2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5, IL-10 or IL-13.
source: For example, clone DGA4 secreted large quantities of IL-17A, IL-6, TNF-α and GM-CSF, but failed to secrete the prototypic Th2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5, IL-10 or IL-13, and thus displayed an 'atypical' Th17-like phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine profiling data.

claim: Clone TC5A87 released substantial amounts of VEGF and PGDF-AA, but only little Th1 or Th2 cytokines, and no IL-17A.
source: In contrast, clone TC5A87 released substantial amounts of VEGF and PGDF-AA, but only little Th1 or Th2 cytokines, and no IL-17A.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine profiling data.

claim: Four of the seven MR1T cell clones studied displayed a Th2-skewed profile of cytokine release.
source: Notably, four of the seven clones studied (DGB129, CH9A3, DGB70, JMA) displayed a Th2-skewed profile of cytokine release.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine profiling data.

claim: Both control MAIT cell clones showed uniform Th1-biased responses following activation by A375-MR1 cells pulsed with E. coli lysate.
source: In the same experiments, both control MAIT cell clones, although derived from two different donors, showed uniform Th1-biased responses following activation by A375-MR1 cells pulsed with E. coli lysate.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine profiling data.

claim: Both resting MR1T and MAIT cell clones displayed high levels of CXCR3 (with the exception of the DGA4 clone only).
source: Both resting MR1T and MAIT cell clones displayed high levels of CXCR3 (with the exception of the DGA4 clone only; Figure 7B), However, we observed divergent expression patterns of CCR4 and CCR6 (Figure 7B), which further suggested that MR1T cells are heterogeneous and different from MAIT cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Divergent expression patterns of CCR4 and CCR6 were observed among MR1T and MAIT cell clones.
source: Both resting MR1T and MAIT cell clones displayed high levels of CXCR3 (with the exception of the DGA4 clone only; Figure 7B), However, we observed divergent expression patterns of CCR4 and CCR6 (Figure 7B), which further suggested that MR1T cells are heterogeneous and different from MAIT cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Mo-DC and THP-1 cells were recognized by the majority of the tested MR1T cell clones.
source: Mo-DC and THP-1 cells were recognized by the majority of the tested MR1T cell clones, followed by the Huh7 hepatoma cells, the LS 174T goblet-like cells and the HCT116 colon carcinoma cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: All MR1T cell responses to cells expressing constitutive surface levels of MR1 were blocked by anti-MR1 mAbs.
source: Importantly, all responses were blocked by anti-MR1 mAbs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The representative DGB129 MR1T cell clone induced up-regulation of the maturation markers CD83 and CD86 on Mo-DCs.
source: The representative DGB129 MR1T cell clone reacted to Mo-DC from different donors (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) and induced up-regulation of the maturation markers CD83 and CD86 on these target cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Mo-DC maturation promoted by DGB129 cells was fully inhibited by anti-MR1 mAbs.
source: Remarkably, Mo-DC maturation promoted by DGB129 cells was fully inhibited by anti-MR1 mAbs, thus confirming that recognition of MR1 was required for this T helper-like function.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The JMA MR1T cell clone reacted to LS 174T by secreting in MR1-dependent fashion IL-8 and IL-13.
source: The selected JMA MR1T cell clone reacted to LS 174T by secreting in MR1-dependent fashion IL-8 and IL-13 (Figure 8D,E), two cytokines involved in the modulation of human intestinal epithelial cell functions (Iwashita et al., 2003; Sturm et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 8D and 8E.

claim: JMA recognition of LS 174 T cells promoted increased transcription of mucin 2 gene (MUC2), which was prevented by anti-MR1 blocking antibodies.
source: Interestingly, JMA recognition of LS 174 T cells also promoted their reciprocal activation resulting in increased transcription of mucin 2 gene (MUC2), which was prevented by anti-MR1 blocking antibodies (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by Q-PCR data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The total volume of the MR1 antigen-binding pocket is far larger than any of the MR1 ligands reported to date.
source: The total volume of the MR1 antigen-binding pocket is far larger than any of the MR1 ligands reported to date, suggesting capacity to bind a wider repertoire of antigens than that known so far.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of MR1.

claim: MR1 has capacity to bind a wider repertoire of antigens than that known so far.
source: The total volume of the MR1 antigen-binding pocket is far larger than any of the MR1 ligands reported to date, suggesting capacity to bind a wider repertoire of antigens than that known so far.
evidence: This is inferred from the large size of the MR1 antigen-binding pocket.

claim: MR1T cells represent between 1:2500 and 1:5000 of total circulating T cells.
source: Using as APCs A375 cells expressing high levels of MR1, we estimated that MR1T cells represent between 1:2500 and 1:5000 of total circulating T cells.
evidence: This is calculated from flow cytometry and cloning experiments.

claim: The calculated range of MR1T cell frequency could be underestimated as A375 cells utilized for the frequency studies might lack some MR1T cell antigens.
source: The calculated range of MR1T cell frequency could however be underestimated as A375 cells utilized for the frequency studies might lack some MR1T cell antigens and therefore fail to stimulate a fraction of MR1T cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential limitations of the frequency estimation method.

claim: MR1T cells might be activated upon metabolic changes in target cells induced by environmental signals, infection or cell transformation.
source: It is tempting to speculate that these cells might be activated upon metabolic changes in target cells induced by environmental signals, infection or cell transformation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the potential physiological role of MR1T cells.

claim: Some activated MR1T cell clones displayed atypical functions for T cells, including the release of growth factors VEGF and PDGF.
source: Interestingly, some activated MR1T cell clones also displayed atypical functions for T cells, including the release of growth factors VEGF and PDGF, which support mesenchymal cell proliferation, vasculogenesis, and angiogenesis (Carmeliet, 2003), suggesting a potential role in tissue remodeling processes.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine profiling data and citation to prior work on VEGF and PDGF functions.

claim: MR1T cells may have a potential role in tissue remodeling processes.
source: Interestingly, some activated MR1T cell clones also displayed atypical functions for T cells, including the release of growth factors VEGF and PDGF, which support mesenchymal cell proliferation, vasculogenesis, and angiogenesis (Carmeliet, 2003), suggesting a potential role in tissue remodeling processes.
evidence: This is inferred from the release of VEGF and PDGF by some MR1T cell clones.

claim: MR1T cells might drive inflammatory responses, support B cell function, mediate DC licensing, promote tissue remodeling, and contribute to mucosal homeostasis.
source: Based on the diversity of effector molecules they release following antigen stimulation, MR1T cells might drive inflammatory responses, support B cell function, mediate DC licensing, promote tissue remodeling, and contribute to mucosal homeostasis by enhancing innate defenses at the epithelial barrier.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the diverse effector molecules released by MR1T cells.
